content: King County Library System needs a central administration module for its multi-branch Integrated Library System. System administrators should be able to configure library processes, manage users, groups, and privileges, monitor and troubleshoot servers, databases, applications, services, and interfaces, coordinate software updates, and protect operational data through backup and recovery. The module must support centralized administration without disrupting daily library services.

The administration function is mainly responsible for keeping the whole library system running in a coordinated way across all branches. That includes managing users and access, setting up operational rules and processes, monitoring the health of servers and services, coordinating updates, and making sure backups and recovery are in place so we can protect data and keep service available.
From a business standpoint, the goal is to give system administrators one central place to manage the system without each branch having to handle technical administration on its own. It supports day-to-day operations by reducing interruptions, helping staff resolve issues faster, and making sure changes can be applied consistently across the branches while normal library service continues.

Yes, definitely. Right now a lot of the pain is around having to touch multiple systems or branches separately, which creates duplicated work and slows down simple changes like access updates or configuration changes. There’s also some confusion at times about who owns a problem when it affects more than one branch, so we want the central function to make responsibilities clearer and help us respond faster when something goes wrong.

On a day-to-day basis, we’d expect it to manage things like user accounts, roles and privileges, branch-level configuration, system settings, audit logs, and operational status data from servers, databases, applications, and interfaces. We’d also want it to keep track of backup and recovery information, and likely update or maintenance records too.
That data would be used to make administration consistent across branches, to troubleshoot problems faster, and to give administrators a single view of what’s happening in the environment. It should also support reporting and auditing so we can see who changed what, when, and whether the system is healthy.

In general, the central administration module should be the authoritative source for shared system records like users, permissions, global settings, and core operational status. Branches might have their own local settings or service-specific notes, but those should stay separate unless they are meant to be standardized across the system.
I wouldn’t expect branch data to override the central record by default. If there are exceptions, they’d have to be clearly defined by policy, because we want to avoid conflicts and accidental overwrites.

It needs to respect our access control rules first, so only authorized staff can make changes, and some actions should require elevated approval. It also has to preserve auditability, meaning we can see who changed a record and when, and it shouldn’t let one branch accidentally affect another branch’s local operations unless that change is meant to be system-wide.
We also need it to follow our retention and privacy expectations for operational data, especially anything tied to staff accounts or troubleshooting logs. If a process would interrupt public service, that should be avoided or at least scheduled carefully.

Yes, we would want normal configuration changes limited during busy service periods and during major update windows, so branches aren’t disrupted during the day. I don’t know that we have fixed freeze dates for everything, but there are definitely times when changes should be held back unless they’re urgent.
If something urgent comes up outside those periods, it should still be possible for authorized staff to make the change with proper approval or an emergency path, and the system should record that it was done outside the normal window.

Yes, some branch-specific settings should stay local by default, especially things tied to a branch’s daily operations, like local service hours, staffing-related configuration, or branch-specific notices. Those shouldn’t automatically ripple out to other branches.
A change should only affect multiple branches or the whole system when it’s clearly marked as a shared standard, comes from an authorized central administrator, and follows whatever approval process we set for broader impact.

They’ll need enough training to understand the difference between local, branch-level actions and system-wide changes, plus how approvals and audit trails work. I’d also want them to be comfortable recognizing when a change could affect service at multiple branches, because that’s where mistakes can be costly.
The system should make the common tasks easy to learn, like updating users or checking system status, but it should make high-impact actions more deliberate so people don’t do them by accident.

They should definitely treat anything that changes permissions, security settings, authentication, backup and recovery settings, or core integrations as high-impact. The same goes for changes to shared catalog, circulation, or notification configurations if those are centralized, because those can affect service across branches pretty quickly.
They should also pause for anything that could take a server, database, or interface offline, even briefly, or anything that would overwrite or bulk-update records. In those cases, I’d expect them to seek approval or use an emergency process if service is already at risk.

High-impact changes should normally require approval from someone with administrative authority, and for especially risky changes I’d expect a second set of eyes from IT or a designated supervisor. I don’t think regular staff should be able to self-approve those changes unless they’re already authorized for that level of access.
Bypassing the normal path should only happen in a real service-threatening situation, like a system outage, security issue, or data recovery need, where waiting would create more harm. In that case the emergency process should still require logging what was done, why it was necessary, and who authorized it afterward.

Version upgrades definitely need approval and extra review, especially if they touch the core application or database. Security patches are important too, but those might move faster if the risk of delaying them is higher.
Any update that could affect integrations, interfaces, or service availability should be treated as high-impact as well, including dependency changes and configuration changes that come along with the update. The key is whether the update could interrupt service, change behavior in a noticeable way, or require coordination with branches.

Yes, we would expect some sequencing rules, but I don’t know that they’re fully defined yet. In general, anything that depends on another component should be updated after the dependency it relies on, and anything that touches shared data or interfaces should be coordinated carefully so we don’t break transactions or messaging.
Parallel updates might be okay for unrelated components, but only if we’re confident they don’t share dependencies or create downtime together. If there’s uncertainty, I’d expect the safer path to be sequential with confirmation between steps.

If the change only affects that branch’s own staff, workflow, or local settings and doesn’t touch shared services, it should be able to proceed independently. If it changes something that other branches rely on, like a shared catalog rule, circulation policy, user privilege, or an interface, then it needs coordination or a wider change.
The main exception would be if the local change is actually part of a centrally approved standard that has to be rolled out everywhere, or if it’s a temporary workaround that reveals a system issue we need to fix centrally. In that case another branch might be affected because the “local” issue is really system-level.

If the same change is likely to be repeated at other branches, that’s a sign it should probably be centralized. I’d also treat it as central if staff are working around a limitation in the system, because that usually means the root problem belongs with the shared configuration or application, not the branch.
Another clue is if the change affects reporting, authentication, permissions, or any shared workflow that central admins already govern. In those cases, even if one branch noticed it first, it’s probably not really a local change.

For the initial release, the main outcome is that central admins can keep the whole library system running without disrupting branches, so the essentials are user and privilege management, basic process configuration, monitoring, troubleshooting, and backup and recovery. Day to day, they need to be able to see what’s going wrong, fix access issues, coordinate updates, and recover data if something fails.
A feature is essential if not having it would prevent safe administration of the system or create an unacceptable risk to service. If it mainly improves convenience, automation, or reporting detail, I’d say that can wait for a later release.

If an update is limited to a branch-specific workstation or something that doesn’t connect to shared services, it can usually be applied locally. If it touches the core ILS, shared databases, authentication, interfaces, or anything that could affect more than one branch, it should be scheduled centrally so the timing and rollback plan are controlled.
If there’s a chance it could interrupt circulation, catalog access, patron services, or messaging between systems, then it should wait for a maintenance window or a low-risk period. Anything that looks unstable or untested enough to threaten branch operations should not be pushed just because it’s convenient.

Most branch-specific day-to-day settings should probably stay local, especially things like local notices, workstation-specific preferences, and minor workflow options that only affect one branch. If a function is low risk and doesn’t affect shared data or other branches, local staff may be better positioned to handle it quickly.
That said, I’d still want central control over anything that affects security, patron data, circulation rules, or system integrations. Those are the areas where inconsistency would create too much risk.

Access should be role-based and limited to people who actually need it for their job, with stronger restrictions on anything that can be changed versus just viewed. Sensitive records like audit logs, account details, and backup information should be visible to administrators and support staff only when they’re handling a legitimate operational issue, and even then the write access should be tightly controlled.
If the data includes patron or security-related information, I’d expect masking or partial display unless someone has an approved reason to see the full record. And if someone outside the normal admin role needs access for troubleshooting, that should be temporary and logged, with escalation through the appropriate support process.

I don’t know the exact retention period offhand, because that usually depends on county policy and legal requirements, so we’d need to verify that with the team. In general, I’d expect staff account and troubleshooting data to be kept only as long as needed for operations, audits, and incident follow-up, then archived or deleted according to policy.
Privacy handling should be stricter for anything that can identify a person or reveal system behavior in a security-sensitive way, so access should stay limited and logged. Longer retention or fuller access would make sense when there’s an active incident, a compliance hold, or a formal investigation that requires the records.

If the record affects security, shared workflows, or system-wide behavior, the central administration module should stay the source of truth. Branches or other systems can request the change or supply the input, but the central module should own the authoritative update so everyone stays consistent.
I’d only allow another system to write directly if it’s clearly the designated owner of that data and there’s a controlled integration in place. If ownership is unclear, or if two places could disagree, then central control should win.

A second approver should be required for changes that could affect many branches, alter security permissions, interrupt service, or change core circulation or integration settings. I’d also expect dual approval for anything that is hard to roll back or has a real chance of impacting patron service if it goes wrong.
An emergency change could be made before approval only if it’s needed to restore service or reduce immediate risk, like during an outage or security incident. Even then, it should be logged, time-limited, and reviewed afterward so the approval isn’t bypassed permanently.

The timing should depend on how critical the data is and how much delay the library can tolerate. For things like account or circulation-related updates, I’d expect near real-time or frequent syncing, while less urgent data can run on a schedule to reduce load.
If an interface is sensitive or the downstream system is busy, it may need to be delayed or queued so we don’t overload shared services. Event-triggered sync makes sense when a specific action happens, like a patron update or status change, as long as the integration can handle it reliably.

If the change directly affects patron service, it should be prioritized and run as soon as the system can safely handle it. If either system is under heavy load, I’d expect the change to be queued rather than dropped, unless it’s truly nonessential and can wait for the next cycle.
When there’s a risk of overwhelming a downstream system, slowing the sync is better than forcing it through, because consistency is less useful than stability. The main rule should be to protect service continuity while making sure critical updates still get through in a timely way.

For those kinds of high-impact changes, I would not want the second approver skipped in normal circumstances. Once a change can affect multiple branches, security, core circulation, integrations, or patron service, dual approval should be the default.
The only exception I’d be comfortable with is a true emergency where service restoration is the priority and there isn’t time to wait, but even then it should be documented and reviewed after the fact. I wouldn’t make that a routine shortcut.

If the issue is clearly cross-branch or tied to a shared service, central should take ownership right away because one branch can’t really coordinate that on its own. If it’s local but has ripple effects, the branch can lead initially, but central should be pulled in quickly to coordinate and avoid conflicting actions.
The practical rule is whoever has the best visibility and authority over the impacted service should own the response, while the other side stays informed and supports. If response speed matters, we’d still want a quick handoff path so ownership doesn’t get stuck in debate.

Staff account records should be kept only as long as they’re needed for active employment, audit, or security purposes, and access should be limited to administrators who need it for their job. Troubleshooting logs should also be time-limited, with tighter access because they can contain sensitive system details or user-related information.
I’d expect longer retention for anything tied to audits, security incidents, or unresolved operational problems, but only with stricter access controls. If a log or record is no longer needed, it should be deleted or purged according to policy rather than kept indefinitely.

Yes, anything that shows system health, error details, or interface activity should be handled more carefully because it can expose a lot about the environment. Those logs and monitoring records should have tighter access than ordinary administrative data, and we’d want a clear audit trail of who viewed or changed them.
I’d also expect different retention depending on the purpose: short retention for routine diagnostic logs, but longer retention for incident investigation or compliance needs. If a record is tied to an external interface or security issue, it should probably be treated as more sensitive than standard operational data.

Access should be limited to administrators and support staff who are actively responsible for monitoring or resolving the issue, and only for the systems they need to touch. If the record contains security-sensitive details, that should be even more restricted, with audit logging on every view or change.
In practice, I’d expect role-based access with a need-to-know approach, so not every system admin automatically sees everything. If someone doesn’t need the detail to do their job, they shouldn’t have access to it.

Those records should be treated as highly sensitive by default, with access limited to the smallest support group that can work the issue. If they need to be shared wider for investigation, that should be temporary and deliberate, not the normal state.
Retention should be extended only as long as the investigation, audit, or legal need exists, and then the records should be disposed of under policy. Every access, export, or change should be logged, because those are exactly the cases where we’d want a strong audit trail.

They should be able to inspect status, review logs, restart services, clear stuck jobs, and verify connectivity or configuration when needed. In some cases they may also need to disable or re-enable an interface, but that should be controlled because it can affect branch operations.
Anything that changes data or has a broad service impact should be more tightly restricted and probably require additional approval or at least a clear audit trail.

If the action only affects one branch’s own local environment, it can stay local as long as it doesn’t impact shared services or other branches. If it touches a shared server, central database, common interface, or anything that could cascade to multiple branches, then it should be treated as system-wide and handled centrally.
The practical line is whether the change has isolated impact or shared impact. If there’s any real chance it could affect more than one branch, I’d want central review or control before it goes ahead.

A branch can keep ownership if the issue is clearly rooted in something local and the other-branch impact is only indirect or not yet confirmed. But once there’s credible evidence that a shared service, central database, or interface is involved, I’d expect central ownership to take over.
In practice, branch staff would still be part of the response, but the central team should lead anything that can spread beyond one branch. That keeps the response coordinated and avoids conflicting changes.

Anything that can interrupt branch operations should be limited to authorized administrators with a clear operational need, and ideally done during a low-impact window if timing matters. For disabling or re-enabling an interface, I’d want an explicit approval step or at least documented authorization, because that can stop transactions or delay updates.
It should also be visible to other support staff so they know what was changed and why, and the action should be fully logged for later review. If there’s any doubt about impact, central operations should have to sign off before it happens.

Yes, I’d defer anything that isn’t needed to run or support the system safely on day one, especially nice-to-have reporting, advanced analytics, or highly customized automation. The rule should be whether the capability is essential for administration, troubleshooting, security, or recovery of the library system.
If it’s core to keeping branches operating or protecting operational data, it belongs in the initial release. If it adds convenience but doesn’t reduce risk or keep the system running, it can wait.

The initial release should include the operational data needed to administer users, groups, privileges, configurations, system status, logs, and backup or recovery information. That’s the information support staff needs to keep the library system running and to trace problems when something goes wrong.
I’d keep out anything that’s purely analytical, historical in a deep-retention sense, or tied to convenience features rather than operations. Sensitive records should still be included if they’re necessary, but only with the access, retention, and audit controls we discussed earlier.

If it directly helps keep branches running, restore service, protect data, or manage access safely, I’d treat it as operationally necessary for day one. If the system can still be supported without it, and staff would just be working more efficiently or with better convenience, then it can be deferred.
When it’s truly gray, I’d use the risk test: if leaving it out creates a real chance of service disruption, data loss, or security problems, include it now; otherwise push it to a later release.

For the core operational data, I’d expect a very short recovery point objective, probably close to real time or at least no more than a few minutes of loss, because losing admin changes or status data could make recovery harder. Recovery time should also be short, on the order of minutes to a couple of hours depending on the size of the failure, since the administration module is there to keep the system running.
Yes, the targets should vary somewhat by data type and scenario. For configuration, access, and audit data, the tolerance should be tighter than for less critical logs, and a full server failure would naturally allow more recovery time than a minor service outage.

For the most critical operational data, I’d say every update should be captured essentially immediately. Changes to access, configuration, and recovery-related information are the ones you really cannot afford to lose, even for a few minutes.
The only exception I can think of is if something is clearly transient or informational and doesn’t affect the actual state of the system, but for anything that changes how the system operates, I would not accept a deliberate gap.

Yes, we’d need retention rules that keep change history and status records long enough to support audits, troubleshooting, and accountability. I’d expect the record to show who made the change, when it happened, what was changed, and ideally the before-and-after values for important settings.
I don’t know the exact retention period yet, because that usually depends on county policy and any legal requirements, but the detail should be preserved as long as the record is kept. For operational logs, we’d probably need enough history to investigate incidents without making the system overloaded with unnecessary old data.

Yes, different kinds of records should probably have different retention periods. Security-related changes, privilege changes, and anything tied to incidents or compliance should be kept longer than routine status data, because those are the records people are most likely to need for audit or investigation.
I don’t know the exact time periods offhand, but the rule should be that we keep records as long as they may still be needed for audit, legal hold, or recurring troubleshooting, and only archive or delete them after that window closes. Anything with legal or incident value should be protected from deletion until it is formally cleared.

Archiving should happen when the record is no longer needed for day-to-day operations but still has audit, history, or troubleshooting value, while deletion should only happen when the retention period has expired and there’s no remaining business, legal, or operational reason to keep it. If a record is still needed but rarely accessed, archiving makes sense; if it’s no longer needed at all, then it can be deleted under policy.
Yes, any open audit, legal hold, incident review, or ongoing troubleshooting case should extend retention beyond the normal threshold. In those cases, the record should be locked from deletion until the hold is cleared or the case is closed.

Only authorized roles should be able to place or clear a hold, usually system administrators or a designated records/compliance authority, and I’d want that action to be logged with who approved it and why. Clearing the hold should require the same level of authority as putting it on, or at least a formal approval trail.
While deletion is blocked, the record should still be readable for audit or investigation, but it should not be editable in a way that breaks the evidence trail. If changes are necessary, they should create a new version or append-only history rather than overwrite the retained record.

In an emergency, I could see allowing a senior operations lead or incident commander to place a hold if the normal approver isn’t available, especially if we’re dealing with an active outage or security issue. That would need to be documented right away, with the reason, time, and who took the action, and then reviewed afterward by the regular authority.
Clearing a hold should be stricter. Even in an emergency, I’d expect formal approval and written justification before anything is released, because once it’s gone we can’t get that evidence back.

Every audit log entry should at least include the user ID or role that performed the action, the exact timestamp, the action taken, the record or case affected, and the stated reason or ticket number behind it. For changes to the hold itself, it should also capture the previous state and the new state, so we can see what was actually altered.
If it’s an approval-based action, I’d also want the approving person or authority recorded, plus any reference to the incident, audit, or legal matter that justified it. That way we can reconstruct the full chain later without guessing.

My preference would be to block direct edits to the held record itself and allow only append-only notes or a new version through a controlled update process. That keeps the original evidence intact while still letting staff add context, corrections, or follow-up information if needed.
If there are fields that absolutely must change, like a status flag or a case classification, those should be very limited and tightly controlled, with the old value preserved in history. Attachments tied to the held record should usually be treated the same way, meaning no replacement or deletion unless the system is preserving the prior version.

I would only allow attachment changes if there’s a clear compliance or privacy reason, like redacting personal data, and even then the original should be preserved in a protected form. Replacement or versioning could be allowed if the new file is clearly linked to the old one and the system keeps both versions with the full history.
Deletion should basically not be allowed while the hold is active unless legal counsel or a designated records authority approves it and the action is fully documented. Any such change should record who approved it, what was changed, why it was necessary, and keep an immutable trail of the original attachment and all versions.
